summary: Describes four extra FTP commands that BBN added to its servers so that users can create and remove directories, print the current directory, and move up to the parent directory. They were designed to work on systems with tree-like directories, such as Unix, Tops-20 and Multics.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo proposes four FTP commands for directories: create one, remove one, show the current location, and move to its parent. It also explains why a server should return the full path after creating a directory.

questions: how do you create directories in ftp
what are the ftp directory commands
subtitle: Four FTP commands for creating, removing, and navigating directories.

tldr.problem: FTP users on systems with hierarchical directories needed commands for creating and navigating directories across differing pathname conventions.
tldr.mechanism: The memo proposes XMKD, XRMD, XPWD, and XCUP, and recommends that successful directory creation return an absolute path in reply code 257.
tldr.outcome: The commands are presented as experimental extensions for directory-oriented file transfer. The reply to XMKD helps clients refer to a new directory consistently.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 775's status as Unknown and records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo describes the commands as experimental.

sections.title: Four Directory Commands
sections.content:
The authors added directory commands to FTP servers on Unix systems and sought commands that could also work with tree-like directory systems such as Tops-20 and Multics. XMKD creates a directory, XRMD removes one, XPWD prints the current working directory, and XCUP changes to the parent directory.

Unless the argument carries enough information to specify another location, XMKD and XRMD operate on a subdirectory of the current working directory. Pathname syntax varies by server.
sections.plainLanguage: FTP gains commands to make and remove folders, show where the session is, and move up one level. A directory name is interpreted using the server's own pathname rules.

sections.title: Returning a Usable Directory Path
sections.content:
A newly created directory may not be reachable using the same relative name given to XMKD. This is especially important where the server's naming syntax requires an absolute path or where relative paths depend on the current directory.

On successful XMKD, the server should return a line with code 257, the directory name in quotes, and optional commentary. The reply must contain the absolute pathname. Embedded quotation marks are doubled. XPWD also uses 257 on success because it returns the same kind of path information.
sections.plainLanguage: After creating a directory, the server reports its full path. The client can then use that exact name even if the server treats relative names differently.

sections.title: Reply Codes and Compatibility
sections.content:
The memo recommends that XCUP use the same reply codes as XCWD and that XRMD use those of DELE. It lists command-specific replies for success, unsupported actions, access denial, invalid or ambiguous paths, and file-system errors. Reply 257 is the only new reply code for the earlier FTP protocol discussed in the memo.

For XMKD, a directory that already exists is treated as an error. The server should also deny creation if a file with the same name conflicts with the directory. These choices are intended to make directory-tree transfer work across systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The new commands reuse familiar FTP replies where possible. A successful create or directory listing uses 257 and includes the path.
